title: Why the comparison is COHR and LITE, but the analog is something smaller
body:
## The Scale Gap Is Not the Point

The first instinct when a European semiconductor company announces US dual-listing preparations is to benchmark it against the American-listed incumbents in the same vertical. In co-packaged optics, that reflex leads directly to Coherent Corp. (COHR) and Lumentum (LITE) — two companies that in March 2026 received a combined $2 billion in simultaneous strategic investments from NVIDIA, a vote of confidence that rippled through every laser and transceiver stock on both sides of the Atlantic.

The size comparison is arresting. Coherent reported quarterly revenue of approximately $1.81 billion in its most recently disclosed quarter, implying an annualised run-rate above $7 billion. Lumentum's comparable figure was roughly $808 million per quarter, tracking above $3 billion annually. MACOM Technology Solutions — a third US-listed photonics semi that frequently appears in the same analyst notes — generates approximately $700 million annually. Against these: Sivers Semiconductors reported full-year 2025 net sales of SEK 306.6 million, approximately $33 million at prevailing exchange rates. Sivers is roughly 1% of Lumentum's revenue base and less than half a percent of Coherent's. By revenue, this is not a David-and-Goliath story. It is a David-and-skyscraper story.

That framing, however, mistakes the competitive question. Sivers is not competing for Coherent's transceiver integration business or Lumentum's optical amplifier franchise. It is positioned — aspirationally, at this stage — at a specific, narrow layer of the supply chain that is structurally reorganising as the industry migrates from pluggable transceivers toward co-packaged optics.

## What Changes at the CPO Layer

In a pluggable transceiver architecture, lasers are effectively commoditised within well-defined categories. Transceivers ship in standard form factors. Customers specify speed and reach; manufacturers produce to catalogue. The large integrated players — Coherent, Lumentum — are optimised for exactly this world, as are the high-volume Japanese generics: Furukawa Electric and Sumitomo Electric, which mass-produce standardised continuous-wave lasers for the bulk transceiver market. Volume, cost efficiency, and yield across millions of units are their competitive axes.

Co-packaged optics disrupts this in a structural way. When lasers move from pluggable modules into the package itself — directly adjacent to the switch silicon — the specification requirements diverge from anything in a standard catalogue. Each customer's interposer geometry, thermal envelope, channel count, and wavelength grid is bespoke. The External Light Source must be tuned to the specific optical platform it feeds. Sivers' own product literature emphasises "customised III-V lasers for specific customer specifications" — language that maps precisely to what POET Technologies, Ayar Labs, and O-Net require from their laser supplier. Whether that custom-specification layer carries durable pricing power against the integrated giants' resources is the open question the chapter cannot resolve.

## The Counterargument Has Substance

Both integrated giants are moving into expanded InP capacity — and faster than the CPO chokepoint thesis would prefer. Coherent disclosed in its FY26 results that it had doubled 6-inch InP wafer output one quarter ahead of its own schedule. Lumentum has acquired a fifth InP fabrication facility in Greensboro, North Carolina, converted from GaAs — a capital commitment unambiguously targeted at expanding custom laser supply. These are not the moves of companies that have ceded the high-specification layer to European design houses.

A further credibility flag on Sivers' own numbers: its PCAOB-restated financials — prepared as part of the US dual-listing process — widened the FY2025 operating loss from SEK 141 million to SEK 178 million and *reduced* FY2024 revenue by SEK 24 million relative to originally reported figures. The restatement drivers included revenue reallocation between periods, revised inventory valuations, and impairment of previously capitalised development expenditures. The accounting gap between Swedish K3 standards and PCAOB requirements is not trivial, and it narrowed the equity base from SEK 1.08 billion to SEK 950 million. Sivers enters the US listing process with a cleaner balance sheet — and a wider disclosed loss.

## The Real Comparable: MACOM, Not Coherent

The more instructive competitive frame is not Coherent or Lumentum but MACOM Technology Solutions — the Lowell, Massachusetts-based photonics semi that occupies a structurally analogous position: a publicly traded laser-chip pure-play with an explicit CPO laser supply positioning, not attempting to compete in transceiver assembly.

| Company | Annual Revenue | Market Cap | Revenue Multiple |
|---|---|---|---|
| Coherent (COHR) | ~$7.2B | ~$19B | ~2.6× |
| Lumentum (LITE) | ~$3.2B | ~$8B | ~2.5× |
| MACOM | ~$700M | ~$10B | ~14× |
| **Sivers Semiconductors** | **~$33M** | **~$2.2B** | **~67×** |

The table captures the core tension. At SEK 72.90 per share across 311.3 million shares outstanding — currently at its five-year high — Sivers is priced at roughly 67 times revenue. To reach MACOM's revenue run-rate, Sivers would need to multiply its top line approximately 20 times. The analyst bull-case model in current specialist investment commentary projects SEK 2.3 billion in 2030 revenue at a 25% operating margin, implying a fair-value estimate of SEK 14.52 per share. The gap to the current market price suggests investors are pricing a scenario considerably more aggressive than even the optimistic case — or pricing a strategic acquisition premium before any acquirer has emerged.

## Geography as an Unpriced Variable

One factor absent from standard comparable-company analysis but material to any complete competitive map is geographic. Sivers is Swedish and British — its photonics subsidiary operates from Glasgow. Coherent is American, with a Swedish operational element. Lumentum and MACOM are both American. Furukawa and Sumitomo are Japanese. From the perspective of a hyperscaler constructing a CPO supply chain for the late 2020s — under conditions of US-China technology bifurcation and potential East Asian supply concentration risk — a European-headquartered independent InP laser source has structural value that does not appear in a discounted cash flow model. The $6.6 million Year 2 grant from the US Microelectronics Commons programme, announced in May 2026, is at least consistent with the thesis that Western government entities view Sivers as a strategic supply option. Whether that optionality justifies a $2.2 billion equity valuation is a separate calculation.

## The Historical Pattern, and What It Requires

The competitive template that Sivers' investment thesis implicitly borrows is well-established in semiconductor history. EML laser specialists who captured the 100G-to-400G transceiver transition built the design-win foundation that became Lumentum's current franchise. Applied Optoelectronics captured disproportionate upside in the 800G and 1.6T transceiver assembler cycle during 2025 by being the right-size, right-specification supplier at the precise moment hyperscalers were racing to lock up bandwidth-density supply. In each case, the winner was not the largest player in the adjacent vertical — it was the one whose specific product specification aligned with the inflection that was actually occurring.

Sivers is positioned at the equivalent inflection for CPO DFB lasers. The preconditions for execution are demanding: a named hyperscaler production order, a successful fab ramp from Glasgow, and a financing structure that avoids forced dilution before revenue arrives. Shares outstanding have already doubled since 2020. The POET partnership — early prototypes expected in H1 2026, production readiness targeted year-end — is the nearest-term test of whether the pattern applies.

The competitive position is asymmetric in both directions. Sivers can lose if Coherent and Lumentum expand custom-laser capability faster than CPO adoption creates lock-in, if Furukawa or Sumitomo upgrade their large-scale production to architectural CW-CPO grades, or if a hyperscaler decides the laser layer is too strategic to outsource. Sivers wins disproportionately to its current revenue base only if one of the POET, Ayar, or O-Net partnerships converts to a named hyperscaler production order before the window narrows. The current market price already assumes a version of that outcome — leaving limited room for the execution risk that the financials, and the restated financials in particular, are signalling is real.
